World.title: Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan sends congratulatory letter to President Ilham Aliyev
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, May 22. Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan, the Vice President, Deputy Prime Minister, Minister of Presidential Affairs of the United Arab Emirates, has sent a congratulatory letter to the President of the Republic of Azerbaijan, Ilham Aliyev, Trend reports.

"Honorable Mr. President,

I am pleased to express my sincerest congratulations and best wishes to Your Excellency on the occasion of the Independence Day of Azerbaijan.

I wish you robust health and happiness, and the Government of Azerbaijan and the friendly people of Azerbaijan progress and prosperity.

Please accept the assurances of my highest respect and esteem for Your Excellency," the letter reads.

World.title: ​D-8 Secretary-General discusses accelerating launch of three regional centers in Baku
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, May 22. The Secretary-General of the Developing-8 Organization for Economic Cooperation (D-8), Ambassador Sohail Mahmood, conducted his first official visit to Azerbaijan on May 17–20, 2026, to attend the 13th Session of the World Urban Forum (WUF13) and advance plans for three new regional hubs in Baku, Trend reports.

Organized upon the invitation of President Ilham Aliyev, the high-level visit focused on strengthening economic integration, aligning sustainable urban planning with renewable energy goals, and reviewing preparations for the 12th D-8 Summit in Jakarta.

​A major outcome of the diplomatic mission was the reinforcement of progress toward launching three specialized institutional platforms in the Azerbaijani capital: the D-8 Energy and Climate Center, the Transport Center, and the Media Excellence Center. During high-level consultations, Assistant to the President Hikmat Hajiyev and Foreign Minister Jeyhun Bayramov discussed Azerbaijan’s expanding strategic role and ongoing institutional reforms to boost the financial capacity of the D-8 Secretariat.

​Energy Minister Parviz Shahbazov and Mahmood finalized operational frameworks for the upcoming Baku-based Energy and Climate Center ahead of the First Meeting of D-8 Energy Ministers in Baku on June 1, 2026. Additionally, the Secretary-General coordinated with Ahmad Ismayilov, Executive Director of the Media Development Agency, to structure professional exchanges and joint capacity-building programs through the new Media Excellence Center.

At the forum, Mahmood proposed a five-pronged cooperation strategy encompassing digital governance, green infrastructure investment, and regional designations like the "Sustainable D-8 City of the Year" to incentivize clean energy transitions across the 1.28-billion-population bloc.

World.title: Building townhouses on a residential Canberra block could soon be easier
World.content:
Townhouses, terraces and low-rise apartments will be allowed on all ACT residential blocks if new planning rules pass in the legislative assembly.

The ACT government's proposed changes to the Territory Plan will allow any block with a single home to be developed with multiple townhouses or terraces.

Block consolidation and subdivision will also be permitted, and developments up to three-storeys high would be permitted on some blocks that already allow townhouses.

ACT Planning Minister Chris Steel said the proposed changes were intended to enable 30,000 new homes in the territory by 2030.

Planning Minister Chris Steel says many of Canberra's existing urban areas can take on more housing. (ABC News: Callum Flinn)

"It's part of a significant change to the Territory Plan, the most significant since self-government, to enable more homes," Mr Steel said.

"The missing middle is about providing more homes in between large-scale multi-unit apartments and single detached dwellings.

"These reforms will mean that townhouses, terraces, multi-occupancy dwellings and low-rise apartments would be permitted in existing RZ1 and RZ2 areas in the territory."

Mr Steel said the changes would enable more housing choice across the capital to avoid limiting medium-density housing options to new or outer suburbs.

"Canberra is a very low density and spread-out city, and so many of our existing urban areas can appropriately take on more housing," he said.

"We're not expecting every single block in every single street to be developed overnight. This will occur over many decades.

"It's a significant change, but one that we expect to see over the medium and longer term."

Under the proposed changes three-storey developments will be allowed in more suburban areas. (ABC News: Mark Moore)

Mr Steel added the proposed changes would be helpful for a variety of Canberrans at different stages of life to find appropriate housing.

"This is an important reform for people who are looking to get their first step on the housing ladder," he said.

"It's important for families that want a place that's slightly larger than an apartment.

"And it's important for older Canberrans who want to age in place in the community that they love."

Mr Steel said that factors like street parking, open spaces, and the existing character of suburbs would be taken into account.

Canberra streetscapes 'well protected'

David Shearer of SPACELAB says Canberra's streetscapes are well protected and unlikely to be significantly changed by densification. (ABC News: Mark Moore)

Director of projects at SPACELAB urban design and town planning, David Shearer, said Canberra was certainly in need of more missing middle housing.

"At the moment we've got a lot of Canberra suburbs that are losing population," Mr Shearer said.

"They're losing vitality, and they're sort of dying at the core.

" So missing middle [housing] will revitalise a lot of those suburbs, bring life back to them — and that's got to be a big benefit. "

He said he didn't believe Canberra's streetscapes would change very much as a result of the proposed reforms.

"All of these policies take a long time to flow out, to see a lot of change happen anywhere, and streetscapes are well protected in Canberra," he said.

But Mr Shearer expressed concerns the current taxation policy for housing developments were not in line with the proposed planning policy.

David Shearer of SPACELAB says missing middle housing could help revitalise Canberra suburbs. (ABC News: Stuart Carnegie)

"At the moment taxation policy — being the Lease Variation Charge — is driving development outcomes that are completely not in alignment with the missing middle," Mr Shearer said.

" Unless LVC is redesigned or literally thrown in the bin and a better design invented for development contributions, the missing middle will stay missing. "

Mr Steel said the government was currently reviewing that tax system as part of the budget, and changes in line with the proposed Territory Plan reforms were more than likely.

"We'll be looking at how we can encourage more people to take up these missing middle housing opportunities, recognising that the tax may impact on the viability of development," Mr Steel said.

'Don't want to see the character of our suburbs trashed'

Canberra Liberals Leader Mark Parton said his party was broadly in favour of the reforms, but he would be looking at the details carefully.

"I think it's extremely important that we get the controls correct," he said.

"We've been focusing on that up until this point, and we'll continue to focus on it because we don't want to see the character of our suburbs trashed."

Canberra Liberals Leader Mark Parton says it's important to get the controls right on the proposed planning changes. (ABC News: Monte Bovill)

Mr Parton added that while he understood concerns about development making suburbs too dense, those concerns had to be balanced with the need to house Canberra's growing population.

"I'm extremely mindful of the impact that some of these townhouse developments could have on individual blocks," he said.

"But I'm also mindful of the fact that not everything can stay the same.

"The city is growing, and some things have to change."

The government is due to respond to an assembly inquiry and finish public consultations on the proposed missing middle housing reform by July.

World.title: Rural women share harrowing IVF stories at parliamentary inquiry
World.content:
All Sophie Fletcher wants is to complete her family, but her journey has been a long and harrowing one.

She has endured miscarriages, false hope and seemingly endless hours of travel throughout her IVF (in-vitro fertilisation) journey.

The ripple effect travels through her family, including her five-year-old son Dougal.

"He's very well versed in embryo transfers and miscarriage and infant loss now," Ms Fletcher said.

"If he sees me crying it's, 'Mummy, did the baby die?'

"He's learning things that no five-year-old should really have to."

Sophie Fletcher says her family's lives have changed forever after her IVF journey. (ABC News: Genevieve Blandin de Chalain)

The Walcha farmer and mother of two travels six-and-a-half hours interstate for her treatment, in the hope of completing her family.

She then turns around to make the long trip back to Walcha.

"It's an extra layer of mental load and torture, essentially it's torturous what you've got to go through living out here," Ms Fletcher said.

Those experiences were shared at a parliamentary inquiry that sat in Tamworth this week.

The select committee inquiry into fertility support and assisted reproductive treatment was established last year.

Sophie Fletcher hopes changes will come from the inquiry. (ABC News: Genevieve Blandin de Chalain)

Ms Fletcher said it was confronting to relive her experiences, but she did it in the hope that better support systems would be created as a result of the inquiry.

"A cheat sheet would be nice, even just finding out which pathology places you can go to get same-day results," she said.

"There was a lot of trial and error on my part, a lot of error going to places that told me they would have same-day results but in fact it would be three days before we got them, which impacts your cycle."

Armidale mum Kirra Smith said her journey to fall pregnant with her son, Raymond, was a long one.

She agreed that same-day blood results were crucial for IVF but told the inquiry that, because of her location, that was not possible.

Kirra Smith says her IVF journey left her feeling isolated. (ABC News: Genevieve Blandin de Chalain)

"We can't get same-day bloods here in Armidale. They get sent to Tamworth in a little courier and then they get on a plane to go to Sydney, and in that time they may have missed my ovulation," Ms Smith said.

Ms Smith said if her access to care had been different, she might have been able to avoid serious health issues that resulted in hospitalisation.

"Maybe I wouldn't have got ovarian hyperstimulation and I wouldn't have had to spend a week in Tamworth's Intensive Care Unit," she said.

"I like to hope that something like that could be avoided if we had same-day bloods."

Kirra Smith has travelled over four hours from her farm outside Armidale to receive IVF care. (ABC News: Genevieve Blandin de Chalain)

Stories 'powerful' to hear

Listening to the harrowing tales that Kirra Smith and Sophie Fletcher shared was select committee chair Sarah Mitchell.

The shadow minister for health said the personal accounts were upsetting.

"The more that you speak to people … there does seem to be challenges that just don't exist for people who live in the city," she said.

Sarah Mitchell says hearing the experiences of rural women was emotional. (ABC News: Liam Patrick)

" We've got to do better and I think it's been really important to hear those stories. "

Ms Mitchell said there were many challenges to overcome.

"The distances to travel, the leave, the cost involved; it all really adds up," she said.

"I think also when it comes to IVF access, just the fact that there aren't any public IVF clinics outside of Sydney is a real challenge.

"That will really help the committee as we go through the process and look to make some recommendations to government."

Giving rural women a voice

Jen Laurie is the founder of Her Herd podcast and a perinatal and paediatric mental health clinician based in the New England region.

Jen Laurie says rural women need to have a voice at the table. (ABC News: Genevieve Blandin de Chalain)

Ms Laurie told the committee was also behind the Bush Babies Campaign, which called for an inquiry into the decline of rural and remote maternity services.

"From conception at home or whether or not you have to take significant trips down the highway in order to access IVF services, it's really important that we give regional, rural and remote Australia a voice at the table," she said.

"Our job today is to make sure that rural people are at the forefront of recommendations.

"Really looking at continuity of care, the fragmented service, proper subsidies for travel and proper funding for public services."

World.title: 'Life is football' here but without money, Australia's most unique club won't survive
World.content:
Willie Rioli Jr — a gemstone in the treasure chest of Australian football history, a prince of the Australian Football League's most majestic family — is sitting under a billowing tree in Wurrumiyanga, sweating, exhausted, content.

Warning: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander readers are advised that this story contains the name and image of a person who has died.

7.30 has permission from Willie Rioli Senior's family to use his name and image.

It is half-time during his first football game on the Tiwi Islands since he was a boy.

Teammates nibble icy poles.

Coach Patrick Bowden paces and studies his whiteboard with brother Rhett.

A white-haired spectator rests against the tree, almost fainting, astounded that anyone could actually play in this heat.

At a rare home game, in a pre-monsoonal atmosphere, locals desire victory and rain.

Rioli Jr is shirtless, a small 2018 West Coast Eagles premiership tattoo on his ribs, thinking of his late father, Willie Sr, who died in 2022 at age 50.

A small 2018 West Coast Eagles premiership tattoo on Willie Rioli's ribs. (ABC News)

Up here, Willie Sr was a player, coach, mentor, role model, friend, legend.

Today, his son has a strip of brown tape on his wrist, where he has written "DAD".

Still only 30, Willie Jr is considered by some as the best kick in the family, the highest praise given the Riolis' mastery of the Sherrin.

He kicked 151 goals in his 109 games with the Eagles and Port Adelaide, each one of them seemingly inevitable, executed with superior evasion and splendid timing.

Willie Rioli Jr after winning the 2018 AFL Premiership with West Coast. (Quinn Rooney/Getty Images)

He was also a defensive weapon.

Anyone can see the value of his presence in a replay of the last two minutes of the 2018 grand final: centre square repeat effort, tackling Jeremy Howe in the goal square, a first-year player slamming the door shut on Collingwood and its army.

Giving back after footy took away

He could still be playing in the AFL, earning good money.

Willie Rioli was still pivotal in playing footy at the highest level shortly before his retirement. (James Elsby/AFL Photos via Getty Images)

Instead, he came home.

"For me, it's just timing," Rioli Jr tells the ABC.

"Mum's been a bit crook lately and she sacrificed a good 15 years for me to live out my dream of playing AFL footy — and I've seen the last few years with dad not being around she's been struggling, so it's my time to give back to these kids and spend quality time with my mum and my kids as well."

Willie Rioli is grateful to be back home and spending time with his mother. (ABC News)

Giving back to family is a Tiwi trait, a Rioli tradition.

Family supported him in his rise to fame, and family stood by him in crisis, including a plea of guilty for a cannabis possession charge in 2021, and his father's fatal heart attack a year later.

Rioli Jr's career had some rocky patches off the field. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

He considered quitting.

Even in this "dark time" he was conscious of his role model status.

"I do hold a bit of blame myself a little bit for some of the stuff I have been through, in terms of clubs not trusting Indigenous players," Rioli Jr said in 2025.

"I felt that was my driver to come back to footy … be the light in terms of 'we can go through this'.

Willie Rioli hopes to inspire the next generation of Indigenous AFL players. (ABC News)

"I look at the drop in terms of Indigenous players in the competition; that gives me the motivation to stick around longer, to help the next generation do better than what we are doing or what I am doing. It's more just trying to show the real person I am.

" I want the next [Indigenous] generation to be better than what we are right now. And I want them to have their confidence to make mistakes and not be judged by their mistakes. "

Willie Rioli and Bobby Hill during the All Stars game in 2025. (Dylan Burns/AFL Photos via Getty Images)

His final year of professional football was angst-ridden.

He was racially abused online for expressing his dislike of Hawthorn Football Club, due to "deep-seated pain and sadness from past family experiences", and he was criticised for sending a confrontational private message to an opponent, Western Bulldogs defender Bailey Dale.

But it was his mother Georgina's health, his father's legacy, and his sense of passing time that decided his future.

Rioli sees playing with the Tiwi Bombers as an opportunity to give back. (ABC News)

"I've got no bad blood with the AFL," he tells the ABC at Wurrumiyanga.

"I love what they do with our people. I left the AFL with good terms.

"For me now, it's just giving back to these kids, hopefully giving them guidance that we never had when we were young.

"Football's a journey. The people you learnt off along the way that helped shape you into a better person, a better player … because where I come from, as you can see, we're raw out here, raw talent.

"I feel like our next generation will be better."

From a young age kids get out to the football ground on the Tiwi Islands. (AAP Image: Lucy Hughes Jones)

Football is a way of life on the Tiwi Islands. (AAP Image: Lucy Hughes Jones)

Under the tree at half-time, his mind turns to winning a game for the Bombers, a one-of-a-kind footy club founded almost 20 years ago to combat world-worst rates of youth suicide.

He begins to deliver an address to teammates, a lesson in top-level strategy, and they stop moving to listen.

"We're working hard to slide and support," he says. "The more we slide and support, the more our backs are gonna intercept it and we're gonna go, go back at the game."

Coach Bowden, of Alice Springs origin, who played 75 AFL games, watches with pride. He first coached Willie Jr as a teenager in Perth — their relationship has spanned a generation and continent.

Patrick Bowden coached the junior Rioli before he headed to the AFL. (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

"See a blue jumper … just go there," Willie Jr instructs.

"Go to the corridor. If we protect the corridor, they've got nowhere else to go. Go out there, tackle, chase, that's all we need."

Loading...

Witnesses are in awe of this precious football moment — as a returning hero shares the wisdom from his there-and-back-again journey.

"This is an experience like no other, really," Bowden confides as his players follow Rioli back onto the field.

" I say my bit, but when Willie talks, it's really special and the boys listen. He's got control of them now. "

Rioli-inspired, the Bombers surge, finding a state of dynamic balance in which the beautiful chaos of Tiwi football is somehow synchronised.

Many of the younger players on the Tiwi Islands look up to Rioli. (ABC News)

A nine-goal victory is celebrated by locals, and the sky promises big rain tonight.

Asked by this over-heated spectator if he is "a born coach", Rioli Jr says he wants to be.

"My dad taught me to lead and sometimes I don't lead by talking as much, but football is my strength, I know a lot of these kids — when I talk they listen," he says.

Willie Rioli Senior while playing for South Fremantle in the late 80s. (Supplied: WAFL Collectables)

" I feel like it's time for me to give back and no better space to come back home and be here in front of my people. "

'Life is football' but Tiwi footy is in trouble

Rioli Jr's homecoming to the Tiwi Bombers came as the club approached its 20-year anniversary.

There is no other footy club like it in what is a footy-mad nation.

Patrick Bowden's brother Sean is AFLNT chairman. He says the Bombers "are integral to the Northern Territory Football League".

The Tiwi Bombers Football Club celebrates its 20th anniversary in 2026. (ABC News)

" On the Tiwi Islands, life is football. "

But the Bombers face significant logistical and financial challenges.

There are three separate training venues (Darwin, Bathurst Island, Melville Island), and getting men's and women's teams to Darwin for most of their games can be arduous in extreme weather.

Many players are Darwin-based, so even the Bombers' few home games take careful planning.

The Bombers face significant logistical and financial challenges when it comes to match preparation. (ABC News)

If the ferry is cancelled due to rough seas, flights have to be organised.

The cost of those can be high and finance is a major problem for the Bombers.

Sponsorship is not what it used to be and a search is underway for more financial help beyond "short-term deals and the kindness of donors".

"The hurdles we face are unlike those of any other club in the country," club secretary Karl Mayne says.

"We are operating one of the most unique and complex sporting models in Australia, and we simply cannot do it on passion alone anymore.

"We've seen many of our foundation funding avenues fall away over the years.

"For the Tiwi Bombers to see another 20 years, the magic on the oval must be matched by stability off it."

Logistical challenges have put a financial strain on the club. (ABC News)

The club has lodged a $300,000-a-year grant application with Aboriginal InvestmeNT.

"We are currently navigating a storm of rising logistical costs and a shifting funding landscape," Mayne explains.

"The reality is that the current model, relying so heavily on a volunteer base to manage such a high-expenditure operation, is unsustainable.

" We need philanthropic leaders and corporate Australia to step up and ensure this pathway for Tiwi talent doesn't disappear. "

Despite their financial woes, Sean Bowden is confident the Tiwi Bombers have a strong future.

"We're committed to continuing the journey," he says.

"And continue to help individual young men and women further their football careers and better their lives."

Funding for two AFLNT-employed football development officers to live and work on the Tiwi Islands comes from government and AFL headquarters.

20 years fighting suicide

While some fight the financial battle, other volunteers are trying to serve the club's original purpose of creating incentive and hope for disadvantaged youth.

Club champion and current assistant coach Simon Munkara remembers how the club began in the mid-2000s.

"The old people were putting this together and made the Tiwi Bombers team for not only us to play but for the young ones coming through and for our future," he says.

Tiwi Bombers men's captain Kim Kantilla watched those first few seasons as a boy.

Tiwi Bombers men's captain, Kim Kantilla (centre) remembers the start of the club. (ABC News: Jack Fisher)

"All I can remember is that there was a lot of suicide," he says.

Kantilla is the great grandson of David Kantilla, first Tiwi Islander to play in the big time (SANFL) in 1961.

"The elders came together and said we need to do something about it and stop the suicide rate. It's very important because you have someone, a coach or another player that you trust."

The earliest days of the Tiwi Bombers were successful; by 2008 the islands' suicide rate had dropped; a first premiership was celebrated in 2012.

But the underlying social challenges remain.

Last year, three Tiwi Bombers players (two males and one female) died by suicide.

Another young player attempted suicide, but his life was saved.

Despite that outgoing club president Lindsay Whiting has been a resilient leader.

Lindsay Whiting is the outgoing club president. (ABC News)

"I was a firm believer and I still am a firm believer that that the football will come," he says.

"As long as at a management level we can do what we need to be able to do to move these kids and support these kids as best as we could.

"I believe in what we're doing with values and morals and things we're trying to instil in our kids.

"To be able to able to motivate these kids in every direction, whether its social, behavioural, healthier choices all of those sorts of things. Sport plays a massive role."

Dreaming of Dreamtime

The Bombers were named after the Essendon Football Club, which has a strong affiliation with the Tiwis through former players Dean Rioli and Michael Long.

And Essendon says they remain committed.

"The partnership between Essendon and Tiwi Islands is built on a genuine investment in people, in culture and in the long-term future of football on Tiwi," Essendon said in a statement.

In 2015, Willie Rioli Sr, as coach of the Tiwi Bombers, was a special guest at the MCG for 'Dreamtime at the 'G'.

Willie Rioli Sr also coached the Tiwi Bombers. (Supplied: Tiwi Bombers Football Club)

"There's a lot of things to take in but it has been very enjoyable," Rioli Sr said then.

"It means a lot. Being a Tiwi person and an Indigenous person of Australia — it's a great thing that the AFL recognises us. It's amazing how big this week has become."

The AFL club still regularly arranges visits and programs for development of players and coaches.

On the day of Rioli Jr's homecoming game, two Essendon's young guns, Issac Kako and Jayden Nguyen, were in Wurrumiyanga playing kick-to-kick with the local kids — trying to knock mangoes from the trees.

Jayden Nguyen spent some time on the Tiwis watching footy. (Getty Images: Russell Freeman)

There's even more opportunity for those kids now.

A post-COVID initiative was the creation of a women's team, unearthing AFLW prospects and empowering many young mothers.

Current co-coach Lilly Carpenter says: "When I first started helping we didn't have much that was happening for the women because a lot of us used to play in Darwin with other sports so it was good finally that the women over here could do something.

The creation of the Tiwi Bombers women's team has empowered many young women and mothers. (ABC News: Jack Fisher)

" We've come far, we wanted to set a foundation for our younger generations coming through. "

And after a lean patch during the pandemic, when it was sometimes hard to field a side, the men's team has returned to prominence

In the 2024-25, season the Bombers came within 10 points of a preliminary final, losing to St Mary's in a semi-final to remember — Anthony Munkara (Simon's nephew and former Essendon rookie) and Billy Munkara (Simon's son) kicking half the Tiwi goals.

But player pathways have somewhat dried up with less Indigenous players now in the AFL than in previous years.

The Tiwi Bombers are one of the most unique football clubs in Australia. (Tiwi Bombers)

"It's something that we want to work on," Indigenous St Kilda star Brad Hill says.

" We want to get more Indigenous players at AFL level. There's obviously something going on – I don't know if it's at grassroots or wherever it is – but we definitely need to put some things in place to get the numbers. "

One place to look is the Tiwi Islands, where the talent is bright as ever.

Earlier this month the Northern Territory Under 16 girls team was announced for the National Championships.

Representing the Tiwi Bombers were Taniesha John-Forrest and Maria Tipuamantamerri.

Last weekend another Tiwi Bomber teenager, Frances Tipungwuti, kicked two goals for the Northern Territory Academy against the Western Jets in the AFL's premier Under 18 competition.

"Frances is a real talent," Patrick Bowden told the NT News over summer. “He’ll go as far as he wants to go.”

Willie Rioli Jr wants to continue to be a leader for peopl on the Tiwi Islands. (ABC News)

And there is another Rioli on the horizon.

Kailanie Rioli, who boards at school in Adelaide, is a member of the Northern Territory Academy Under 18 team.

She is the niece of Willie Rioli Jr, who is committed to helping the next generation rise.

"I think it's just time to give back to these kids," he says.

" Nothing is given, so I just want to hopefully rub it into these kids that if you want to play AFL, you wanna have a good job, you've got to work hard. "

World.title: Fracking could open the door to 10 years of gas supply but is there a risk?
World.content:
South Australia's energy minister says gas reserves under the Limestone Coast may be enough to meet the state's demand for a decade, but an analyst foreshadows companies may not want to explore for it.

The South Australian government this week introduced a bill to lift a 10-year moratorium on fracking in the state's south-east two years early, though it is expected to be defeated in the upper house.

Energy and Mining Minister Tom Koutsantonis said his department "conservatively estimates" about 200 petajoules of known gas reserves in the onshore Otway Basin in SA.

"That's about 10 years' worth of the strategic gas supply that the state government procured [from Santos]," he said.

Tony Beck wants a permanent ban on fracking. (ABC South East: Liz Rymill)

"If you were able to get 20 petajoules a year out of the ground for 10 years, that's the equivalent of every house and business and commercial operation in the state just from one region.

" That would create an oversupply of gas in South Australia, which would lower all of our energy prices. "

Farmers call for protection

The proposal has been met with significant opposition from locals.

Tony Beck, whose family had farmed in the region since the 1950s near Mount Gambier, said farmers in the region were not willing to accept any risk to groundwater.

"I know the engineering, I know the geology, I know what fails and why," he said.

The moratorium is set to expire in late 2028. (Supplied: Beach Energy)

"That experience is precisely what tells me that deep fracking here is a different order of risk [to other parts of the state] entirely.

"Our knowledge of what the risks are and what's being put at risk way outweighs any engineering solutions and the regulatory framework Tom Koutsantonis is relying on."

Mr Beck said he would like to see the moratorium replaced with a more permanent solution.

"Someone should have the courage to bring forward a bill to ban fracking in the south-east permanently," he said.

Mr Koutsantonis said the government would not permit any projects to put the underground aquifers at risk.

Tom Koutsantonis says the government won't put the south east's groundwater at risk. (ABC News: Lincoln Rothall)

"What interest is it for the government to destroy an aquifer?" he said.

"We want those [industries] to survive and succeed, and we would do nothing to hurt the reputation of the manufacturers down there and the raw materials they use to make those goods."

Risk vs reward for companies

Josh Runciman, lead Australian gas analyst at the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis, said he was surprised by the move, given the federal government's announcement of a national reservation policy.

"That reservation policy, if properly designed, should address those supply concerns," he said.

"Lifting the fracking ban may not actually lead to any new gas supply in South Australia anytime soon anyway.

"Geological surveys certainly do suggest there could be gas that could be accessed with fracking.

"But a really important part of the process of identifying commercially recoverable gas reserves is you need to drill to understand how much gas is there and how hard it is to extract."

Josh Runciman says exploring for unconventional gas can cost tens of millions of dollars. (Supplied: IEEFA)

Mr Runciman said it was not unusual for exploration wells in areas that had never been fracked before to cost as much as $20 to $40 million.

"Fracking is fairly expensive, even more so when you're just starting out," he said.

" Potentially [a company] might face a cost well over $100 million just to determine if the gas is commercially recoverable or not. "

Beyond money, Mr Runciman said the time taken to explore and gain approvals to bring gas to the market would also be a factor.

"When we look at eastern Australian gas demand, we see that demand is falling quite quickly," he said.

"There is that longer-term question, then, about the financial incentives for companies to undertake this analysis and try to frack in the south-east.

"Given that east coast gas demand is falling and has fallen quite a bit over the past decade and is likely to continue to fall, I think there are real questions about whether the south-east will be fracked at all."

A change in approach

Deakin University natural resources law academic Samantha Hepburn said she believed the desire to remove the moratorium had several motivations.

Samantha Hepburn says the factors that led to the moratorium have not changed over the past eight years. (ABC News: Kyle Harley)

"Of course, [it's] securing future domestic gas supply, it's going to generate royalties and it's attractive financially for governments," Professor Hepburn said.

"That will, of course, attract regional investment and it's likely to align South Australia with that national future gas strategy.

"But that doesn't take away from the fact that it's still highly volatile.

"It cuts across environmental protection and climate policy frameworks that underpinned the implementation of the moratorium to begin with, which haven't changed."

Mr Koutsantonis said regulations and independent experts would ensure projects did not present an environmental risk.

Fracking has been banned on the Limestone Coast since 2018. (ABC South East: Kate Hill)

"This bill doesn't authorise fracture stimulation. It authorises us to begin the consultation about how this process works and what the concerns are so we can plug it into the regulatory process," he said.

"I think this is all a big fight about nothing.

"Let's let the independent experts [and] the independent regulatory framework that has an overarching mandate of 'do no harm' look at this.

"They're the only ones that can give us the appropriate advice."

World.title: Breaking: Tulsi Gabbard resigns as Donald Trump's director of national ​intelligence
World.content:
Tulsi Gabbard says she will step down from her US director of national intelligence role in Donald Trump's administration.

In a letter posted on X, Ms Gabbard said she was resigning to support her husband after his recent bone cancer diagnosis.

Her resignation takes effect on June 30.

US President Donald Trump praised Ms Gabbard for doing "an incredible job" in the role and said Principal Deputy Director Aaron Lukas would serve as acting director.

World.title: Digital tipping prompts on the rise but not all venue owners are fans
World.content:
The sounds of grinding coffee beans and frothing milk overlap with the ding of the register and chatting customers.

Amid the noise inside this regional cafe is another, perhaps unexpected, sound: coins clattering into a tip jar.

"It is surprising the amount of people that do tip," said the owner of Bundaberg's Ritual Espresso Willow McKenzie.

Willow McKenzie says digital tips count towards the cafe's overall income. (ABC Wide Bay: Grace Whiteside)

She said she emptied her tip jar about once a month and shared its contents, usually between $50 and $100, between her staff.

"I nearly didn't even put a tip jar out, but I'm glad I did."

There's also a tip jar beside the till at the River Cruz Cafe a short stroll down the road, but manager Bec Reid said customers were more likely to give tips directly to staff.

Bec Reid and her son Ashden Whyte often work together at the cafe. (ABC Wide Bay: Grace Whiteside)

"My head barista was given a tip of $50," she said.

But with the decline of cash, more Australians are confronted with an automatic tipping option.

Tipping screens are increasingly integrated into the payment technology, popping up when a customer pays via card.

More Australians are being confronted with a default tip prompt. (ABC News: Timothy Ailwood)

While it can be skipped, some feel it contradicts typical Australian hospitality norms.

And anecdotal evidence showed the automatic gratuity prompt made customers feel pressure to tip, according to University of Queensland professor of economics John Quiggin.

"I certainly don't find it appealing myself," he said.

John Quiggin says it's unclear what customers' reactions are to the default tip. (ABC News: Michael Lloyd)

"Restaurants have either accepted that they're going to get less tips or have moved to these default tips.

" So that's almost certainly led to an increase in tipping, but what's not clear is what people's reactions to that process have been. "

When faced with the option, owners of Bundaberg restaurant Water Street Kitchen, Jen and Alex Cameron, decided against adding the tipping prompt to their electronic sales systems.

Alex and Jen Cameron decided against adding a default tip to their electronic payment system. (ABC Wide Bay: Grace Whiteside)

"I don't ever want a guest to feel the pressure to tip," Ms Cameron said.

"It's really lovely when people acknowledge the hard work of our team, but it's certainly not expected."

Mr Cameron said he didn't think tipping culture was prevalent in Australia, unlike in America where paying a gratuity was expected due to low wages.

"Our staff are paid appropriately. They're not heavily relying on tips for their income," he said.

"If guests want to do that [tip] with cash, they'll do it with cash, and if they want it to be electronic, then they'll prompt us to add that to their bill."

Jen Cameron says receiving a tip is lovely, but "certainly not expected". (ABC Wide Bay: Grace Whiteside)

Who benefits from the tips?

The Australian Restaurant and Cafe Association (ARCA) chief executive Wes Lambert said as electronic transactions became the norm, tipping had followed.

"In the past, I would have said that Australia didn't have a tipping culture," Mr Lambert said.

"But since tapping and paying on cards have made it much easier for patrons in restaurants and cafes to tip, tipping is actually up.

Wes Lambert says digital payments make it much easier for customers to tip. (ABC News: Greg Bigelow)

" It is much easier to pick a certain percentage on a screen than it is to try to figure out what a tip would be when you're using cash. "

There are multiple electronic payment service companies available to business owners, many of which offer a default tip option.

Most charge a percentage fee for each transaction, while others charge a monthly fee or offer plan subscriptions.

Back in Bundaberg's hospitality scene, operators said they remained reluctant to adopt the electronic tipping technology.

Cash tipping remains the primary form of tips in many cafes. (ABC Wide Bay: Grace Whiteside)

Ms Reid said she did not want any additional disincentives amid rising cost-of-living pressures.

"I know times are hard, but I just think that's a lot of pressure on the guests," she said.

World.title: ASIO warning before Bondi attack did not single out elevated Hanukkah risk
World.content:
ASIO issued its annual holiday threat assessment less than two weeks before the terrorist attack at Bondi Beach but did not identify heightened risks to the Jewish festival, despite earlier declaring antisemitism as a top "threat to life".

The ABC has learned the December 2 assessment, distributed to police and government agencies, warned that terrorists could target religious festivals like Christmas and Hanukkah, but did not single out distinct risks to Hanukkah celebrations and said violent protests were more likely.

Police and government agencies relied on the intelligence agency's annual holiday season threat assessment to guide security preparations for major events in December and January.

NSW Police assigned only four officers to periodically monitor the Chanukah by the Sea celebration at Bondi, the most prominent Australian event during Hanukkah, despite requests from a Jewish security organisation for a permanent police presence.

Days earlier, the Community Security Group (CSG) had warned police about the "heightened risk" of a terrorist attack at Hanukkah celebrations, including the Bondi event where 15 people were later killed by alleged Islamic State (IS) terrorists.

Police at Bondi Beach seven days after the attack that killed 15 people. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

The royal commission investigating the attack is expected to question ASIO director-general Mike Burgess and police about security preparations for Hanukkah at the next phase of public hearings, starting Monday.

The commission has said ASIO will face scrutiny over whether it "understood and acted" on its own assessments of a likely terrorist attack and ongoing antisemitic violence.

Mr Burgess has previously said ASIO had no intelligence indicating an attack on Hanukkah celebrations was being planned before the Bondi massacre.

For more than a year before the attack, Mr Burgess had publicly warned that a terrorist attack in Australia was probable.

In February 2025, he declared antisemitism ASIO's highest priority "in terms of threat to life" and said the war in Gaza was increasing the terrorism threat.

Mike Burgess is expected to appear at the next stage of hearings of the Royal Commission on Antisemitism and Social Cohesion. (ABC News: Matt Roberts, file photo)

Mr Burgess is also expected to face questions about how the gunmen slipped off the intelligence radar after first coming to ASIO's attention in 2019, and whether a century-low share of ASIO resources devoted to counterterrorism weakened the agency's response.

The commission is also investigating why NSW Police left security planning for the Bondi event to local officers at Eastern Beaches Police Area Command rather than Operation Shelter, a taskforce established to protect the Jewish community.

Elevated threat at high-profile event

Twelve days before the Bondi Hanukkah event, ASIO's "Holiday period 2025-26: violent protest and terrorism threat assessment" document warned that "overtly religious" events could be "considered for targeting by violent extremists".

According to the public version of the commission's interim report, the assessment referenced an October attack on a synagogue in Manchester, in which an IS-inspired terrorist killed two worshippers on the holy day of Yom Kippur.

The assessment warned police that the Middle East conflict could trigger political violence in Australia but said violent protests were "more likely … rather than acts of terrorism".

Further details remain confidential, but sources familiar with the document said that while it identified Hanukkah among the holiday period's religious festivals, it did not single out Hanukkah events as facing a distinct or elevated threat.

Do you know more? Contact Sean Rubinsztein-Dunlop on Signal: @seanrdunlop.01 and on Protonmail: seanrdunlop@protonmail.com

on Signal: and on Protonmail: Please use this form to get in contact with the ABC Investigations team, or if you require more secure communication, please choose an option on the confidential tips page

The massacre unfolded amid a global surge in anti-Western plots and attacks linked to exhortations from IS over the previous two years to target Jewish and Christian religious events in response to the Gaza war.

The royal commission's interim report noted that previous ASIO holiday season threat assessments to police had explicitly warned of risks during Hanukkah, in particular attacks on "Jewish and Israeli interests" in 2023 and "violent protest and provocative activities" in 2024.

ASIO had separately issued an intelligence report in response to the October 2025 Manchester synagogue attack, warning of "the enduring threat to Jewish interests … in Australia", particularly at crowded places and on holy days "leading up to Hanukkah in December".

On December 5, nine days before the Bondi attack, ASIO warned industry and government subscribers to its broader outreach service, which distributes less sensitive threat advice, that crowded events, including religious celebrations, were the most likely terrorist targets in Australia.

Investigating the return of the Islamic State terrorist group For the past two years, ABC Investigations has tracked the Islamic State terrorist group's revival in Australia, identifying key figures, mapping the network and raising questions about the response of police, intelligence agencies and governments.

The royal commission hearings, some of which will be closed to the public, will also scrutinise why ASIO did not re-examine Bondi attackers Sajid and Naveed Akram in the years after investigating their links to a Sydney-based IS cell in 2019.

The pair were later able to legally acquire firearms and travel overseas, including to Central Asia and a former IS hotspot in the Philippines, without attracting renewed scrutiny.

ASIO's original investigation concluded the father and son did not pose a terrorist threat or support Islamic State — an assessment later questioned by former ASIO chief Dennis Richardson, who served as a special adviser to the royal commission until March.

An internal ASIO review has found no intelligence failure or negligence based on the information the agency possessed before the Bondi attack.

ASIO declined to answer questions from the ABC, including whether its holiday threat assessment was adequate and whether it contributed to security gaps at Chanukah by the Sea, citing the ongoing royal commission.

World.title: Sydney Harbour rubbish loads rise during Vivid, Seabin claims
World.content:
The creators behind floating rubbish bins peppered around Sydney Harbour claim rubbish loads rise during the Vivid Sydney arts festival.

About 20 bins located in bays and marinas near the city's CBD collect waste including microplastics from the surface of the harbour.

Seabin chief executive and co-founder Pete Ceglinski said six years of data showed plastic pollution in the harbour spiked during major events.

"At Christmas we start to see more fake grass, but it's from the plastic Christmas trees," he said.

"Chinese New Year comes around we see fireworks paraphernalia ... and Mardi Gras we see more glitter in the water."

Seabin chief executive and co-founder Pete Ceglinski at Sydney Harbour. (Supplied: Seabin)

Mr Ceglinski said large crowds during longer events like Vivid, which runs for three weeks, could have contributed to the amount of rubbish being seen.

"More humans, more rubbish," Mr Ceglinksi said.

More plastic items collected in 2025

Vivid, which started on Friday, is considered Australia's biggest festival and attracts crowds of more than 2 million people across May and June.

Events are held across different venues in the CBD and light installations draw crowds to a number of sites including harbour locations such as the Opera House.

Reporting on the volume of rubbish it collected in the harbour, Seabin found more plastic items captured in the bins during last year's festival than the year before, despite having deployed fewer bins.

The number of bins in the harbour decreased from 32 in 2024 to 20 in 2025.

But a similar weight of marine litter was still collected and individual plastic items doubled during the 2025 Vivid festival compared with the same period of time the previous year.

Microplastics also went up by 19 per cent.

Seabin Sydney Harbour stats Vivid 2024 Vivid 2025 Change Litres of water filtered 870,128,500 707,498,583.3 -19% Kilograms of marine litter removed 1,201.4 1,192.5 -1% Plastic items captured 367,835 484,784 +32% Microplastics captured 213,407 252,937 +19% Plastic items captured per day 11,495 24,271 +111% Bins operating 32 20 -38%

Meanwhile, festival attendance went up slightly from 2.42 million in 2024 to 2.53 million in 2025.

RMIT University environmental scientist Scott Wilson, who was not involved with the Seabin report, said the results showed an increase in plastic loads between Vivid 2024 and 2025.

"This appears to be in line with increasing visitation over the same period," he said.

"However, the analysis would be further aided by the use of data from outside of the Vivid influenced locations. Similarly, data comparisons could be made with rainfall patterns over the period.

"Both these would help in teasing out what may be coming from the Sydney CBD at this time compared to a broader regional level of input and whether there were any weather derived differences between the comparative periods."

An aquatic bin situated in Sydney Harbour draws in plastic rubbish. (Supplied: Seabin)

Rubbish can get into the harbour from direct littering but also via street waste that gets washed in from stormwater drains. That means more rubbish and plastic winds up in the harbour after major rainfall events.

Spikes in plastic pollution captured by Seabin around Vivid in 2024 and 2025 coincided with high periods of monthly rainfall.

Dr Wilson said the report also showed that while some types of plastics, such as microplastics, collected during Vivid 2025 were higher than Vivid 2024, they were lower than the previous month.

Seabin's pollution index — which applies a pollution ranking out of 11 based on how many litres of water are filtered relative to plastic collected — was set at five for Vivid in the past two years.

Dr Wilson said the index score was also the same for the month prior to Vivid in 2025 suggesting pollution levels were similar before the festival.

But, he said, there appeared to be increases in some types of litter items that could be attributed to large crowds from the event.

"There are obvious increases in certain litter items, possibly even accounting for differences in weather and general harbour inputs, during the Vivid period that could only be attributed to the sheer numbers of people visiting the CBD at this time."

Free aquatic bins offered

Mr Ceglinski said Seabin had gone to the state government department that organises Vivid, Destination NSW, to ask for funding for extra bins and form a partnership during the festival period.

But the request was knocked back.

"We offered to do it for free for the month of the festival and they rejected that as well," Mr Ceglinski said.

"This year I got an email they're not going to go ahead with any support or partnership with us. They're going to focus on their internal waste footprint."

But Mr Ceglinski thought the organisers and city planners needed to do more about the rubbish items brought by people who attended the festival.

He wanted to see more real-time environmental monitoring related to attendee impacts and more planning and spending to mitigate marine pollution.

A rainbow of plastic objects and wrappers are collected from Sydney Harbour every day. (Supplied: Seabin)

A Destination NSW spokesperson said Vivid Sydney continued to evolve its sustainability measures each year as part of broader NSW government commitments.

"Destination NSW and Vivid Sydney take environmental sustainability seriously and work closely with operational partners, venues, suppliers and government agencies to minimise the festival's environmental impact, including waste reduction, recycling and cleaning across event precincts," they said.

"Vivid Sydney implements a range of waste management and sustainability initiatives across festival sites, including increased cleaning services, recycling infrastructure, reducing single-use plastics where possible, encouraging public transport use and supporting refill and reuse initiatives."

Steps to reduce plastic waste

This year, organisers encourage visitors to:

Bring a reusable water bottle or coffee cup

Avoid single-use plastics

Use mobile ticketing instead of printing

If bins are full, take your rubbish to the next bin or home

Use recyclable paper straws

The event's 2025 sustainability report said its key focus had been the reduction of single-use materials.

"Over 1,500kg of corflute and event plastics were recovered and recycled through established waste partnerships, diverting material from landfill," the report said.

Sydney Harbour contains both plastic rubbish and microplastics which are small fragments. (Supplied: Seabin)

The report also provided water stations which it said prevented 12,058 plastic bottles from being used.

A City of Sydney spokesperson said it also deployed extra cleaning services during the Vivid festival.

"Particularly to the northern end of the CBD, to manage increased bin usage and curb potential overstuffing issues," they said.

"We also install extra mobile garbage bins in key locations in the area to assist in capturing waste and prevent it ending up on the ground and subsequently in the waterways."

Dr Wilson said it would be "naive" to think the current waste management measures for Vivid could not be improved during the event.

"Greater number of rubbish bins may be a solution, but this would need to be accompanied by an event-wide litter and waste education and awareness program," he said.

"Another solution could be the addition of filter baskets or other gross pollutant traps in the stormwater network around the Vivid sites during the event, to prevent litter entering the harbour.

"Generally speaking, elimination of disposable single-use products for large-scale events should be the goal and the move towards reusable and more sustainable options a priority."

The NSW government also plans to introduce a re-use only precinct in the Sydney CBD in late 2027 as part of its plan to phase out single-use plastics.

Rubbish concerns go beyond Vivid

The waste problem in Sydney Harbour is well documented and encompasses more than a single festival.

Laura Stone runs ecotour company Sydney by Kayak in the harbour that encourages its customers to take three pieces of rubbish from the water, or foreshore, every trip.

"Over the past 13 years we've removed more than 41,000kg of rubbish from local waterways through guided clean up paddles and community initiatives," she said.

Laura Stone has noticed more plastic waste on the water during busier periods in the city. (Facebook: Sydney By Kayak)

Ms Stone said her team noticed an increase in rubbish around Sydney Harbour during major events, warmer months and periods of high tourism activity.

"As guides who are out on the harbour almost every single day at sunrise, we often see the 'after-effect' before most people are awake," she said.

"I think part of the solution moving forward is continuing to encourage reusable systems wherever possible, improving event waste infrastructure and helping people make the connection between what happens on land and what eventually ends up in the harbour."

World.title: ‘He’s gotta show something’: Who’s who in Qld Labor’s factions, and how they pick their leaders
World.content:
Analysis PoliticsQueenslandALP ‘He’s gotta show something’: Who’s who in Qld Labor’s factions, and how they pick their leaders James Hall May 23, 2026 — 5:59am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Labor leader Steven Miles has been urged by his colleagues to use the dismal Stafford byelection result as an opportunity to reset the Opposition and fine tune the party’s strategy and cohesion. There are no active discussions to move on Miles, who retains the backing of the party room, but there are frustrations with his lack of progress in the 18 months since the 2024 election. And as a deadline to settle on an alternative premier before the next state poll approaches, a leadership logjam in the dominant Left faction delays a genuine challenge. How the Queensland Labor factions operate. Steven Miles retains support as leader but potential contenders include Shannon Fentiman, also from the Left, and Cameron Dick from the Right faction. Matt Davidson The party retained the seat of Stafford in Brisbane’s inner-north in last weekend’s knife-edge poll, despite an 8 per cent collapse in its primary vote, emerging victorious thanks to Greens preferences.



But a once reliable Labor stronghold has been trimmed to a razor margin of about 1 per cent, with the scale of the swing triggering much soul-searching. The party’s long-held view is a leader needs two years in the role before the next state poll in late 2028, after internal analysis blamed the last election loss on Miles only having 10 months in the premier’s job. But Labor sources told this masthead there’s a lack of clarity about who would replace Miles, with one saying “maybe we would be having that [leadership] conversation a bit earlier” if the successor was clear, while another described a “logjam” of contenders in the dominant Left faction. They hoped the byelection would serve as a wake-up call for Miles and the leadership team to reset and resist being dragged into the gutter by Jarrod Bleijie, the notoriously antagonistic deputy to Premier David Crisafulli.



One senior party room source, speaking to this masthead on condition of anonymity to share internal party matters, said Miles’ attempt to spin the Stafford result was “delusional” and Labor needed to settle on an electable leader before Christmas. “He’s got to show something in the next few months,” the source said. “You’d want to see some skin taken off Crisafulli.” But there are mixed views as to who would replace Miles due to the complex organisational structure of the party’s factions. Left Since 2015, the dominant Left faction has controlled the Labor caucus. It counts 18 of the 36 current MPs as members – allowing Miles to lead with the backing of influential United Workers Union (UWU) boss, Gary Bullock.



Shannon Fentiman, also on the Left but not linked to the dominant UWU, is widely regarded as a strong communicator and noted parliamentary performer. She is viewed by some in the party as a more electable alternative to Miles, but is more progressive and unlikely to gain broad support from the Right faction if the Left is split – as it was when Annastacia Palaszczuk stepped down in 2023. Steven Miles spoke in Stafford on Sunday, alongside Shannon Fentiman. William Davis If Miles were to step down, it is expected Meaghan Scanlon would succeed as UWU’s candidate for leader and would then, in turn, have the numbers with the backing of the Right to overcome a split on the progressive side. But an insider said the looming electoral boundary redistribution, which will result in her Gold Coast seat of Gaven being a notionally LNP seat, has cast doubt over her leadership potential.



The unions within the Left Bullock’s factional power stems from his role in planting UWU candidates in supposedly unwinnable electorates just before Labor won government from Campbell Newman’s LNP in 2015. An astute political operator, he had more accurately predicted the swing towards Palaszczuk than his rivals in the union movement had, allowing UWU to seize control of the party room. Meaghan Scanlon is widely viewed as a future party leader. William Davis With Labor in Opposition, insiders say his influence is waning as the union movement’s base exacts revenge and challenges the controlling manner in which Bullock wields power.



In his place, the mainly public service union Together – through its leader Alex Scott – has slowly been increasing its influence. Its membership base is growing, and it is widely viewed Scott was influential in persuading two MPs, Jennifer Howard and Corrine McMillan, to defect from the Right to join the Left faction last year. One recent example of the power shift came when Bullock was replaced by Together president Sharon Abbott as the convenor for the Left. There is ongoing scuttlebutt Scott is hoping to recruit two more MPs to better contend with the dominance of UWU. But those close to the union boss say his growing influence is not a play to change the leader, given Miles is both a UWU and Together member, and is more focused on wresting control from Bullock to change the party’s strategies and direction.



Right Cameron Dick, the former treasurer in both the Miles and Palaszczuk governments and Right faction leader, is well-known with voters and viewed, along with Fentiman, as an electable alternative. Dick is a strong communicator who’s capable of challenging the LNP in parliament and has been viewed as a potential party leader since before Palaszczuk’s election win in 2015. Cameron Dick is a strong parliamentary performer and well-known across Queensland. Jamila Toderas Filippone But the Right, particularly after the defection of Howard and McMillan, don’t have the numbers to mount a genuine challenge.



Following the Stafford victory last weekend of Luke Richmond, the Right-aligned Australian Workers’ Union member, the faction now has 12 MPs in caucus. Old Guard Despite being the junior faction in the party room with six MPs, the Old Guard has typically voted as a bloc and been instrumental in settling leadership and policy disputes under leader Grace Grace. Despite reports at the time of the party split over youth crime policy, Jonty Bush remains a member of the Old Guard faction. Crucially, there are question marks over how rising star MP Jonty Bush will vote, after she rebelled against the faction earlier in the parliamentary term during heated clashes over youth crime policy.



It was speculated at the time Bush would leave the faction, but she remains notionally with the Old Guard. If her vote isn’t guaranteed, this would mean the Right and Old Guard combined have 17 votes compared to the Left’s 18.
